items.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
items.context: Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine: simple, but there is a hardware ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) adds more machines behind a load balancer: near-unlimited and fault tolerant, but needs stateless services and distributed data.

questions.prompt: What must usually be true of a service before you can scale it horizontally?
choices: It runs on a single big server
It is stateless — session state lives in a shared store
questions.explanation: If a request can land on any instance, no instance can hold user state in memory. Move sessions to Redis, a DB or tokens.

items.title: Load balancing
items.context: A load balancer spreads traffic across instances and removes unhealthy ones using health checks. Algorithms: round robin, least connections, IP hash (sticky). L4 balancers route by IP/port; L7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie.

questions.prompt: Requests have very uneven durations (some take 50 ms, some 10 s). Which algorithm spreads load best?
questions.explanation: Round robin ignores how busy a server is; least connections sends new work to the instance with the fewest open requests.

items.title: Cache-aside
items.context: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the app reads the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and populates the cache with a TTL. On writes, update the DB and invalidate (delete) the cache key. Write-through writes cache and DB together; write-back writes the cache and flushes to the DB later (fast, but data can be lost).

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, after updating a user's row you should:
choices: Delete the cached entry so the next read reloads it
Update the cache first, then the DB, in a separate thread
Leave the cache alone; the TTL will fix it
questions.explanation: Invalidating on write keeps staleness short; updating the cache directly risks races between concurrent writers.

questions.prompt: Which write strategy risks losing data if the cache node crashes?
questions.explanation: Write-back acknowledges before the DB has the data.

items.title: Cache eviction
items.context: When a cache is full it evicts entries: LRU (least recently used) is the common default, LFU keeps frequently used keys, and TTLs expire entries by age. Redis supports allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl and others.

questions.prompt: Which eviction policy drops the entry that hasn't been accessed for the longest time?
questions.explanation: LFU drops the least frequently used; FIFO drops the oldest inserted regardless of use.

items.title: CDN
items.context: A content delivery network caches static assets (images, JS, CSS, video) on edge servers near users, cutting latency and origin load. Cache behaviour is controlled with Cache-Control headers; versioned file names make invalidation easy.

questions.prompt: Your users are global and pages load slowly because of large images. First fix:
choices: Serve static assets through a CDN
Add read replicas to the database
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is distance and bandwidth for static files, which is exactly what CDNs solve.

items.title: CAP theorem
items.context: CAP: when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, or an error) and availability (every request gets a response, possibly stale). Partitions are unavoidable, so the real choice is CP vs AP during a partition.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, an AP system will:
choices: Refuse requests until the partition heals
Keep answering, possibly with stale data
questions.explanation: Cassandra and DynamoDB lean AP; ZooKeeper and etcd are CP.

items.title: Replication
items.context: Leader-follower replication sends all writes to one leader, which streams changes to read replicas. Reads scale out; asynchronous replication means replicas can lag, so a user may not see their own write if the read hits a replica.

questions.prompt: A user updates their profile and the page reload shows the old value. Likely cause:
choices: The read went to a lagging read replica
The cache TTL is too long
questions.explanation: Fix with read-your-writes: read from the leader for a short time after a write, or route that user's reads to the leader.

items.title: Sharding
items.context: Sharding splits data across databases by a shard key. Range sharding keeps ranges together but can create hot spots; hash sharding spreads load evenly but makes range queries scatter. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so adding a node only moves about 1/N of the keys.

questions.prompt: Why use consistent hashing instead of hash(key) % N?
choices: Adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys
It guarantees perfectly equal shard sizes
questions.explanation: With % N, changing N moves almost every key, which is a cache stampede or a massive data migration.

questions.prompt: Sharding orders by created_at month creates one overloaded shard. The problem is:
choices: A hot spot: all new writes go to the latest range
questions.explanation: Monotonic keys concentrate writes. Hash the key or add a high-cardinality prefix.

items.title: SQL vs NoSQL
items.context: Relational databases offer schemas, joins and ACID transactions; they're the default for structured, related data. NoSQL stores (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) trade some of that for flexible schemas and easy horizontal scale at very high write volumes.

questions.prompt: A banking ledger needs multi-row transactions and strong consistency. Best default:
choices: A relational database with ACID transactions
questions.explanation: Money movement needs atomicity across rows. NoSQL fits better for, e.g., huge event or session data.

items.title: Indexes
items.context: A B-tree index turns a full table scan into O(log n) lookups for equality and range queries on its columns. The cost: extra storage and slower writes, because every insert/update maintains the index. Composite indexes follow the left-most prefix rule.

questions.prompt: An index on (last_name, first_name) helps which query?
questions.explanation: Left-most prefix: the index can be used for last_name alone, but not for first_name alone.

items.title: Message queues
items.context: Queues and logs (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS) decouple producers from consumers, absorb traffic spikes and enable async work. Most give at-least-once delivery, so a message can be processed twice — consumers must be idempotent.

questions.prompt: Your consumer charges a card per message and the broker is at-least-once. You must:
choices: Make processing idempotent, e.g. dedupe by a message / payment ID
questions.explanation: Store processed IDs (or use an idempotency key at the payment provider) so a redelivery is a no-op.

items.title: Kafka ordering
items.context: A Kafka topic is split into partitions; order is guaranteed only within a partition. Messages with the same key go to the same partition, so per-key order holds. Consumers in one group share partitions; more consumers than partitions leaves some idle.

questions.prompt: How do you keep all events of one order in sequence?
choices: Use many partitions with random keys
Use one consumer group per event
Use the order ID as the message key
questions.explanation: Same key → same partition → ordered.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and you start 10 consumers in one group. Result:
questions.explanation: A partition is consumed by at most one consumer in a group; parallelism is capped by the partition count.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.context: Rate limiters protect services from abuse and overload. The token bucket refills tokens at a fixed rate up to a capacity, so it allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate. Fixed windows are simple but allow double bursts at window edges; sliding windows smooth that out. Over-limit requests get HTTP 429.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm allows short bursts while enforcing a long-run average rate?
questions.explanation: The bucket's capacity is the burst size; the refill rate is the sustained rate.

items.title: Monolith vs microservices
items.context: A monolith is simplest to build, test and deploy at first. Microservices let teams deploy and scale parts independently, at the cost of network calls, distributed data, observability and operational overhead. Common advice: start with a modular monolith and extract services when a real need appears.

questions.prompt: A 4-person startup with one product is choosing an architecture. Most sensible default:
questions.explanation: Microservices solve organisational and scaling problems the team doesn't have yet.

items.title: Circuit breaker
items.context: A circuit breaker (e.g. Resilience4j) wraps calls to a dependency. After too many failures it opens and fails fast without calling the dependency; after a wait it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through, closing again if they succeed. It stops cascading failures and gives the dependency time to recover.

questions.prompt: What does a circuit breaker do in the OPEN state?
choices: Routes calls to a random instance
Queues calls until the dependency recovers
Fails calls immediately without hitting the dependency
questions.explanation: Fail fast (often with a fallback) instead of piling up threads waiting on timeouts.

items.title: Idempotency
items.context: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not. Payment APIs accept an Idempotency-Key header so a client retry after a timeout doesn't charge twice.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP method is NOT idempotent by definition?
questions.explanation: PUT replaces a resource with the same body every time; POST typically creates something new on each call.

items.title: Back-of-the-envelope QPS
items.context: A day has 86,400 seconds (≈ 10⁵ for quick maths). Average QPS = daily requests / 86,400; size for peak at roughly 2–10× the average. 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 QPS.

questions.prompt: 100 million requests per day is roughly how many requests per second on average?
questions.explanation: 100,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 1,157. Then plan capacity for the peak, not the average.

items.title: Availability nines
items.context: Availability targets are expressed in nines: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year (≈ 43 min/month); 99.99% allows about 53 minutes a year; 99.999% about 5 minutes. Serial dependencies multiply: two 99.9% services in a chain give ≈ 99.8%.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much downtime per year does 99.99% availability allow?
questions.explanation: 0.01% of 525,600 minutes ≈ 52.6 minutes.

items.title: Distributed transactions
items.context: Across services you can't rely on one ACID transaction. Two-phase commit coordinates a commit but blocks if the coordinator fails. The Saga pattern runs a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action (e.g. refund) to undo it if a later step fails; it can be orchestrated or choreographed via events.

questions.prompt: Order → payment → shipping across three services; shipping fails. With a saga you:
choices: Run compensating actions: refund the payment and cancel the order
Ignore it; eventual consistency will fix it
Roll back all three with one database transaction
questions.explanation: Sagas trade isolation for availability; each step needs a defined undo.

items.title: CQRS & event sourcing
items.context: CQRS separates the write model (commands) from read models (queries) so each can be shaped and scaled for its job. Event sourcing stores every change as an immutable event and rebuilds state by replaying them, giving a full audit log; read models are projections of the events.

questions.prompt: In event sourcing, the source of truth is:
choices: The latest row in a table
questions.explanation: Current state is derived; you can rebuild or add projections by replaying the log.

items.title: URL shortener
items.context: A classic design: give each long URL a unique numeric ID (DB sequence or distributed ID generator such as Snowflake) and encode it in base62 [0-9a-zA-Z]. Store short → long in a key-value store and cache hot links; redirect with 301 (cacheable) or 302 (trackable).

questions.prompt: How many distinct codes do 7 base62 characters give?
questions.explanation: 62⁷ = 3,521,614,606,208 — enough for decades at high volume.

items.title: Pagination
items.context: Offset pagination (LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000) is simple but gets slower with deep pages and can skip or repeat rows when data changes. Cursor (keyset) pagination uses WHERE id > last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20: fast at any depth and stable under inserts.

questions.prompt: An infinite-scroll feed with millions of rows and constant inserts should use:
questions.explanation: The DB seeks straight to the cursor via the index instead of scanning and discarding the offset rows.

items.title: Real-time updates
items.context: Short polling asks repeatedly on a timer (simple, wasteful). Long polling holds the request open until data arrives. Server-Sent Events push one-way updates over HTTP. WebSockets give a full-duplex persistent connection — the usual choice for chat and multiplayer.

questions.prompt: A chat app needs low-latency messages in both directions. Best fit:
questions.explanation: SSE is server → client only; WebSockets carry both directions on one connection.
